note: Florence, as the leading Guelf city of Tuscany, was a natural ally of the Lombard League against the Hohenstaufen emperors. Florence sent troops to support the League and benefited from Barbarossa's defeat at Legnano (1176) and Frederick II's struggles with the Italian communes. The Guelf-Ghibelline (papal-imperial) factional divisions that structured Florentine politics throughout the 13th–14th centuries originated in this alignment. The Guelf party's victory over the Ghibellines (expulsion of the Ghibellines after Benevento, 1266) transformed Florence into a Guelf city that subsequently defined itself in opposition to imperial power.

_quarry.structural_significance: Florence's Guelf alliance with the Lombard League establishes the city's anti-imperial political identity; the Guelf-Ghibelline factionalism that follows the League's dissolution shapes Florentine domestic politics for a century; the eventual Guelf victory produces the oligarchic merchant republic that generates the Renaissance
